characters.description: The scholar-princess who now sits as Queen of Alethkar, an Elsecaller among the Radiants. Coldly rational and formidably learned, she weighs the hardest choices of the war with a philosopher's detachment, willing to consider options others cannot bear to name.
characters.name: Jasnah Kholin

characters.description: Dalinar's quiet younger son, a Radiant whose gift lets him glimpse possible futures, a power unsettling even to his allies. Gentle and perceptive, often more comfortable with numbers and patterns than with people, he has found a measure of belonging he never expected among the reborn knights.
characters.name: Renarin Kholin

characters.description: The Shin former assassin, now sworn to Dalinar as a Skybreaker seeking lawful justice rather than blind obedience, and bearer of a strange, hungry living sword. Quiet and self-condemning, he longs to answer for his past and to one day return to the homeland that cast him out.
characters.name: Szeth

characters.description: The aged king of Kharbranth, secretly bound to the enemy god yet still treated as an ally by the coalition. His mind swings between dullness and terrible brilliance from day to day, and he pursues a cold, sweeping plan he believes is the only way to save any fragment of humanity, whatever the moral cost.
characters.name: Taravangian

characters.description: A listener scholar who once helped bring her people into the enemy's service and now moves among the ranks of the reborn immortals, privately doubting the cause she advanced. She carries hidden guilt over her role in her people's fate and secret hopes for a different future for them.
characters.name: Venli

characters.description: Kaladin's former friend from Bridge Four, now a willing servant of the enemy and the murderer of a king. Numbed to his own guilt and drawn to a philosophy that promises freedom from pain, he has become a cold and dangerous instrument of the immortals, at ease with killing.
characters.name: Moash

characters.description: An ancient and cultured Fused, one of the enemy's reborn immortal warriors, renowned among her kind as both a commander and a scholar. Coolly courteous and endlessly patient, she takes a scientist's interest in the nature of power itself and is willing to pursue radical means to bring the eternal war to an end.
characters.name: Raboniel

recaps.ending: The battle for Urithiru is won at bitter cost. Navani, after a long captive contest of intellect with the Fused scholar Raboniel, bonds the tower's guardian spirit and rises as a new Bondsmith, restoring the city's ancient defenses and purging the enemy from it; Raboniel and her daughter die in the process. Kaladin, having spoken the Fourth Ideal and accepting that he cannot save everyone, defeats the enemy in the tower, though his former friend Moash murders the beloved bridgeman Teft, a wound that will not heal. In the spren realm, Adolin's trial wins a measure of alliance and revives his once-dead blade, while Shallan confronts more of her hidden past and the secret society hunting her. Venli quietly leads a group of her people toward freedom. But the book's true turn is catastrophic: as Odium, the god of hatred, moves to discard the ailing King Taravangian, Taravangian instead outmaneuvers and kills him, seizing the divine power for himself. The coalition's most cunning traitor is now a god, one who blends ruthlessness with a terrible sense of compassion, and far more dangerous than his predecessor. A formal contest of champions has been agreed to settle the war on a fixed near-future date, and the newly ascended enemy will spend the interval bending the world toward his design.
recaps.in_short: A year into open war with the god Odium, the coalition and the enemy fight a grinding campaign of raids while Dalinar seeks a way to win. The Fused seize the tower city of Urithiru, suppressing its guardian spirit and trapping Navani, Kaladin, and others inside an occupied stronghold. Navani, held captive, matches wits with the brilliant Fused scholar Raboniel over the secret nature of Light, a duel of science that leads to a weapon able to kill even immortals. Kaladin, worn down and unable to fight openly, shelters survivors in the tower's depths and finally speaks the Fourth Ideal of his order, coming into new power. Far away, Adolin and Shallan travel into the realm of the spren to win an alliance, Adolin standing trial to earn the honorspren's aid and drawing his dead sword back toward life. In the climax Navani bonds the tower's guardian and becomes a Bondsmith, reclaiming Urithiru. Then comes the war's great turn: the dying King Taravangian outmaneuvers Odium, kills him, and seizes his power, becoming a new and far more dangerous god of hatred just as a contest of champions is set to decide everything.

recaps.text: Previously: A reborn Knight Radiant named Kaladin rose from slavery to lead Bridge Four; the artist Shallan Davar became a Lightweaver; and Highprince Dalinar Kholin, guided by storm-visions, reunited his people and recovered the lost city of Urithiru. When the cornered Parshendi summoned a second, dark storm, the world's docile parshmen awoke into the returning enemy's soldiers, and the true Desolation began. Facing the god of hatred, Odium, and his immortal Fused warriors, Dalinar's fragile coalition fought to unite the world's monarchs through an ancient portal network. Dalinar confronted the atrocities of his own forgotten past and grew into a Bondsmith bonded to the spirit of the storm, refusing Odium's temptation and declaring himself Unity to turn back the enemy at the battle of Thaylen Field. But the cost was steep: the Alethi capital fell and King Elhokar was murdered by his embittered former guard Moash, who now serves the enemy; Jasnah took the throne; and the seemingly gentle King Taravangian, still trusted, secretly swore himself to Odium. The awakened singers became a living people again, some free, many enslaved to the Fused, and Odium began steering the war toward a decisive contest of champions.

About a year after the stand at Thaylen Field, the war has settled into a grinding campaign of raids and skirmishes between the coalition and Odium's forces, with neither side able to land a decisive blow. Dalinar searches history and his storm-visions for a strategy that could actually win against a god, while the terms of a future contest of champions loom over everything. Kaladin, exhausted by years of battle and haunted by those he has failed, is pulled back from the front lines and struggles with his own darkness. Navani drives the coalition's scientists to unlock new uses of the mechanical magic that powers their world. Adolin and Shallan prepare for a diplomatic mission into the strange realm of the spren to seek allies, and the enemy quietly sets in motion a bold plan to strike at the heart of the coalition's power.

The enemy seizes the tower city of Urithiru itself. The Fused suppress the ancient guardian that protects the tower and its knights, crippling the Radiants stationed there and trapping Navani, Kaladin, and many others inside an occupied stronghold. Unable to fight openly, Kaladin goes underground, hiding and protecting the wounded and the helpless while the enemy hunts him. Navani is taken captive and forced into a wary collaboration with a brilliant Fused scholar who is fascinated by the true nature of the world's Light. Far away, Adolin and Shallan reach the fortress of the honorspren in the spren realm, where Adolin makes the audacious choice to put himself on trial to win their aid for humanity, and Shallan hunts a hidden traitor within their own party while wrestling with buried pieces of her past.

The struggle inside the occupied tower becomes a contest of wits and will. Navani, held prisoner, matches the Fused scholar discovery for discovery in a dangerous study of Light that edges toward a weapon capable of killing even the immortals. Kaladin's guerrilla resistance in the tower's depths pushes him toward the next oath of his order and a reckoning with what he is willing to sacrifice. Adolin's trial before the honorspren forces both sides to weigh humanity's broken faith with the spren, and his strange devotion to his lifeless blade begins to bear unexpected fruit. Shallan closes in on the traitor among them and on long-hidden truths about herself, while Venli quietly steers her people toward a bid for freedom. On every front the pieces move toward a simultaneous crisis.

Everything breaks at once. Navani bonds the tower's guardian spirit and rises as a new Bondsmith, restoring Urithiru's defenses and driving the enemy out, though the Fused scholar and her daughter die in the reckoning. Kaladin speaks the Fourth Ideal, accepting that he cannot protect everyone, and comes into greater power, but his former friend Moash murders the beloved bridgeman Teft, a loss that guts him even in victory. In the spren realm Adolin's trial wins a measure of alliance and revives his once-dead sword, and Shallan resolves more of her hidden past and the secret society hunting her. Venli leads a group of her people toward freedom. Then the war turns on a single stroke: as the god of hatred moves to cast aside the dying King Taravangian, Taravangian instead outmaneuvers and kills him, seizing the divine power and becoming a new, far more cunning god of hatred. With a contest of champions set to decide the war on a fixed near-future date, the coalition faces an enemy deadlier than the one it thought it was fighting.

characters.description: The King of England, ruling by inherited right and presiding over a formal accusation of treason between two nobles. He is ceremonially confident but must manage a conflict that touches his own court and reputation.
characters.name: Richard II

characters.description: John of Gaunt's son and the Duke of Hereford, who formally accuses Thomas Mowbray of treason, embezzlement, and complicity in the Duke of Gloucester's death. He insists on defending his honor through trial by combat.
characters.name: Bolingbroke

characters.description: A powerful nobleman accused by Bolingbroke of treason and involvement in Gloucester's death. He denies the charges and demands combat to clear his name.
characters.name: Thomas Mowbray

characters.description: Bolingbroke's father, an elderly son of Edward III and uncle to Richard. He values lawful order and family honor, yet his loyalty to the crown limits how far he will oppose the king on his son's behalf.
characters.name: John of Gaunt

characters.description: The widow of the murdered Duke of Gloucester and sister-in-law to John of Gaunt. She urges Gaunt to treat her husband's death as an injury to their entire royal family and seek punishment.
characters.name: Duchess of Gloucester

characters.description: The Duke of York's son and a favorite of Richard. He accompanies Bolingbroke partway into exile despite their political hostility and remains close to the king.
characters.name: Aumerle

characters.description: Richard's uncle and John of Gaunt's brother. He criticizes the king's expensive court and poor counsel while continuing to recognize his lawful authority.
characters.name: Duke of York

characters.description: Richard's queen, deeply attached to her husband. Before his Irish expedition, she feels an unexplained foreboding and fears that approaching sorrow is already present.
characters.name: Queen Isabel

characters.description: A powerful northern lord angered by Richard's treatment of the nobility and Bolingbroke's inheritance. He helps organize support for Bolingbroke's return to England.
characters.name: Northumberland

characters.description: One of Richard's close court favorites. He remains with the queen when the king departs for Ireland and becomes a target of the nobles who blame the favorites for misgovernment.
characters.name: Bushy

characters.description: A courtier favored by Richard and associated with Bushy and Bagot. He helps advise the queen during the king's absence and is condemned by the returning opposition as a corrupt influence.
characters.name: Green

characters.description: A churchman loyal to Richard and the principle of hereditary monarchy. As Richard's authority collapses, Carlisle warns that removing an anointed king will bring prolonged civil bloodshed.
characters.name: Bishop of Carlisle

characters.description: A servant in the Duke of York's household who tends the garden while the queen listens nearby. He interprets the neglected kingdom through the practical order required to maintain plants and trees.
characters.name: Gardener

characters.description: York's wife and Aumerle's mother. Protective of her son, she welcomes Bolingbroke as a kinsman but remains alert to dangers facing her family after the change of power.
characters.name: Duchess of York

characters.description: A nobleman in the new king's circle who listens as Henry wishes aloud for release from the fear posed by the imprisoned Richard. He interprets the remark as a call for decisive action.
characters.name: Exton

recaps.ending: Richard is imprisoned at Pomfret Castle, where he reflects on identity, kingship, and isolation. After he attacks a keeper who reports that the new king has withdrawn a customary privilege, Exton and armed men enter. Richard kills one attacker before Exton kills him. Exton brings Richard's body to Henry IV, expecting approval, but Henry condemns the deed and banishes him, while acknowledging that his own words may have prompted it. Elsewhere, the new king hears that rebels against him have been defeated and pardons the Bishop of Carlisle. With Richard dead and reports of severed heads arriving from the fighting, Henry announces a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to atone for the bloodshed associated with his rise. Bolingbroke holds the crown as Henry IV, but the violence predicted by Carlisle has begun, and the legitimacy of the new reign remains burdened by deposition and regicide.
recaps.in_short: Richard II stops a trial by combat between Henry Bolingbroke and Thomas Mowbray, banishes both men, and later seizes Bolingbroke's inheritance after John of Gaunt dies. While Richard campaigns in Ireland, Bolingbroke returns, claiming only his estate, and rapidly gains noble support. Richard's allies collapse; he submits to Bolingbroke and is taken to London. In Parliament, Bolingbroke presses charges, Richard relinquishes the crown, and Bolingbroke becomes Henry IV. A plot to restore Richard is discovered when York finds his son Aumerle's involvement; Henry pardons Aumerle after the Duchess of York pleads for him. The queen is separated from Richard and sent to France. At Pomfret, Richard is attacked by Exton and killed after fighting back. Henry condemns Exton, although his own words inspired the murder, and plans a penitential journey to Jerusalem as his contested reign begins.

recaps.text: King Richard summons Henry Bolingbroke and Thomas Mowbray to hear their accusations. Bolingbroke charges Mowbray with treason and involvement in the Duke of Gloucester's death; Mowbray denies it. John of Gaunt refuses to pursue vengeance for Gloucester outside lawful royal authority, despite the murdered man's widow urging action. Richard arranges a trial by combat at Coventry, then halts it before the duel begins. He banishes Bolingbroke for ten years, reduced to six after seeing Gaunt's grief, and banishes Mowbray for life. Mowbray laments losing his native language, while Bolingbroke leaves England bitter but controlled. Richard then prepares an expedition to Ireland, already short of money and surrounded by favorites whose influence troubles older nobles.

The dying Gaunt rebukes Richard for exploiting England and wasting its inherited wealth. After Gaunt dies, Richard seizes his lands and revenues rather than allowing Bolingbroke to inherit, alarming York and other nobles because their own property now seems insecure. Richard names York as regent and leaves for Ireland. Northumberland, Ross, and Willoughby learn that Bolingbroke has returned with armed supporters, publicly claiming his lawful inheritance. York lacks the resources and confidence to resist effectively. The Welsh force waiting for Richard disperses after rumors of his death, while the queen's foreboding deepens. Bushy and Green flee toward Bristol; Bolingbroke's party captures and executes them, and the nobles who had supported Richard increasingly join the returning exile.

Richard returns from Ireland and initially trusts that divine kingship and loyal subjects will defeat Bolingbroke. Successive reports strip away that confidence: the Welsh troops are gone, favorites have been executed, York has submitted, and more nobles have changed sides. At Flint Castle, Bolingbroke presents himself as a subject seeking only the restoration of his title and estate, backed by an army. Richard recognizes that he has no effective choice and agrees to go with him to London. The queen overhears a gardener compare the neglected country to an untended garden and learns that Richard is expected to be deposed. Her personal grief now joins the public collapse of his rule.

In Parliament, Bolingbroke demands judgment on the charges surrounding Gloucester's death. The Bishop of Carlisle argues that a lawful king cannot be judged by a subject and predicts civil war if Richard is deposed. He is arrested for treason. Richard is brought in to relinquish the crown publicly. He and Bolingbroke hold it between them before Richard surrenders it, and Richard examines how royal identity dissolves when its ceremonies and authority are removed. He refuses to read a written confession of crimes and asks for a mirror, which he breaks after seeing that his face does not display his inner ruin. Bolingbroke becomes King Henry IV. Aumerle and the Abbot of Westminster then join a secret plan intended to remove the new king and restore Richard.

On the road to confinement, Richard and Queen Isabel share a final meeting. Richard tells her to return to France and preserve his story, while Northumberland forces them apart. At York's house, York discovers a sealed document showing that his son Aumerle is involved in the conspiracy against Henry IV. He rides to expose it despite the Duchess of York's pleas. Aumerle reaches the king first and confesses; York demands punishment, while the duchess kneels until Henry pardons her son. The other conspirators receive no such protection. Henry later speaks of his unease while Richard remains alive, and Exton interprets the remark as a wish for Richard's death. Richard, meanwhile, has been sent to Pomfret Castle.

At Pomfret, Richard tries to occupy his isolation by analyzing his situation, but each reflection returns him to mortality and the loss of kingship. A groom visits and tells him that Bolingbroke rode Richard's former horse at the coronation. When a keeper refuses Richard's accustomed food privilege on orders from above, Richard attacks him. Exton enters with armed servants; Richard seizes a weapon and kills one man before Exton strikes him down. The new king receives reports that the conspirators against him have been killed and pardons Carlisle. Exton then presents Richard's body. Henry condemns and banishes Exton, denying that he ordered the murder even as he recognizes that his own anxious words encouraged it. He announces a journey to Jerusalem to seek absolution. Henry IV possesses the throne, but Richard's blood and the suppression of resistance darken the new reign from its beginning.

characters.description: A wealthy young English bachelor and the narrator. Bertie is generous, sociable, and convinced that he understands human nature, although his efforts to manage other people's romances usually create new complications. He returns from Cannes determined to prove that he can solve his friends' troubles without relying on Jeeves.
characters.name: Bertie Wooster

characters.description: Bertie's exceptionally capable valet. Jeeves is discreet, observant, and skilled at arranging social outcomes, but he and Bertie begin the book at odds over Bertie's new white mess jacket. When Bertie rejects his advice, Jeeves waits with professional calm while events develop.
characters.name: Jeeves

characters.description: Bertie's forceful and affectionate aunt, proprietor of the magazine Milady's Boudoir and hostess at Brinkley Court. She recruits Bertie to present prizes at Market Snodsbury Grammar School and expects him to help preserve peace among her guests.
characters.name: Aunt Dahlia

characters.description: Bertie's shy old friend, whose absorbing interest is the study of newts. Augustus has fallen in love with Madeline Bassett but cannot bring himself to declare his feelings, prompting Bertie to undertake a campaign on his behalf.
characters.name: Augustus Fink-Nottle

characters.description: Bertie's friend and Angela's fiancé at the start of the trouble. Tuppy is hearty, proud, and easily provoked; a careless remark about Angela's appetite has produced a serious quarrel between them.
characters.name: Tuppy Glossop

characters.description: Aunt Dahlia and Tom Travers's daughter. Angela has broken with Tuppy after he compared her unfavorably with another young woman, and she is in no mood to accept an easy apology. She remains close enough to Bertie to become involved in his plans.
characters.name: Angela Travers

characters.description: A dreamy and intensely romantic young woman staying at Brinkley Court, and the object of Gussie's devotion. Her sentimental view of the world makes Bertie's attempts to speak for Gussie unusually dangerous for him.
characters.name: Madeline Bassett

characters.description: Aunt Dahlia's husband and the master of Brinkley Court. Tom dislikes unnecessary expense and is frequently occupied with his collection of antique silver, leaving Dahlia and Bertie to manage the household's emotional crises.
characters.name: Tom Travers

characters.description: The celebrated French chef at Brinkley Court. Anatole's cooking is a major source of household pride, and Aunt Dahlia regards the possibility of losing his services as a disaster. He is also sensitive to unexplained disturbances around his kitchen and quarters.
characters.name: Anatole

characters.description: The experienced butler at Brinkley Court. Seppings carries out his duties amid the guests' schemes and becomes an unwilling participant in the confusion surrounding the prize-giving ceremony.
characters.name: Seppings

recaps.ending: After Bertie's independent schemes have left the couples divided and Brinkley Court in turmoil, Jeeves resumes control. He guides events so that Gussie and Madeline become reconciled and renew their engagement, while Angela and Tuppy also make peace. The threat that Anatole will leave the Travers household is removed, saving Aunt Dahlia from losing her prized chef. These settlements also free Bertie from Madeline's belief that she must marry him if Gussie fails her. Bertie recognizes that his attempt to demonstrate superior judgment has instead proved Jeeves's indispensability. He yields on their private dispute and agrees to give up the white mess jacket Jeeves dislikes. The jacket is then destroyed while supposedly being pressed, completing Jeeves's quiet victory as Bertie returns to his customary dependence on his valet's advice.
recaps.in_short: Bertie Wooster decides to solve two romantic disputes without Jeeves: shy newt-fancier Gussie Fink-Nottle cannot propose to Madeline Bassett, while Tuppy Glossop and Bertie's cousin Angela have quarreled. At Brinkley Court, Bertie's amateur psychology produces mistaken declarations, hunger campaigns, and a perilous understanding that Bertie will marry Madeline if Gussie disappoints her. Gussie, accidentally fortified with alcohol before presenting school prizes, gives a disastrous public speech and loses Madeline's approval. Further schemes disrupt the household and threaten Aunt Dahlia with the departure of her cherished chef, Anatole. Once Bertie finally accepts help, Jeeves arranges reconciliations for both couples, secures Anatole's position, and releases Bertie from Madeline's conditional claim. Bertie concedes that Jeeves has won their contest of judgment and abandons the white mess jacket that began their disagreement.

recaps.text: Bertie Wooster is a well-meaning bachelor whose money and social connections repeatedly draw him into the problems of friends and formidable relatives. His valet, Jeeves, combines wide knowledge with a gift for quiet manipulation and has often rescued Bertie from unwanted engagements and failed schemes. Bertie appreciates the rescues but remains eager to prove that his own judgment can equal Jeeves's. Aunt Dahlia Travers is among Bertie's favorite relatives, though her requests are seldom optional. Tuppy Glossop is both Bertie's friend and a recurring source of friction.

Bertie returns from Cannes wearing a white mess jacket that Jeeves strongly dislikes, opening an unusual breach between master and valet. Bertie then learns that his timid friend Gussie Fink-Nottle is in love with Madeline Bassett but is unable to propose. Confident in his own grasp of psychology, Bertie rejects Jeeves's proposed approach and takes charge himself. Aunt Dahlia also summons him to Brinkley Court, where she expects him to present the prizes at Market Snodsbury Grammar School. A second romantic problem emerges: Angela Travers and Tuppy Glossop have quarreled after Tuppy made an insulting comparison involving Angela's appetite. Bertie sees both disputes as opportunities to demonstrate that he can arrange lives as effectively as Jeeves.

At Brinkley Court, Bertie tries to speak to Madeline on Gussie's behalf. His indirect approach goes wrong when Madeline concludes that Bertie himself is in love with her. She gently explains that she cares for Gussie, but leaves Bertie with the alarming understanding that she may accept him if Gussie proves unworthy. Gussie remains too nervous to act naturally, while Angela and Tuppy maintain their separation. Bertie continues to prescribe emotional shocks and jealousy as cures, despite the fact that those involved do not respond as his theory predicts. Jeeves offers limited assistance but does not take responsibility for a campaign Bertie insists on directing.

Bertie's efforts to reconcile Angela and Tuppy revolve around making each believe the other is suffering, but pride and misunderstanding turn the tactic into a contest of wills. Food becomes part of the scheme, a particularly serious matter in a house where Anatole's cooking is prized. Gussie does at last move closer to Madeline, yet his dependence on Bertie's coaching makes the situation unstable. Bertie is now entangled in every dispute: if Gussie's courtship fails, Madeline may turn to him, while Aunt Dahlia holds him responsible for restoring harmony and fulfilling the prize-day obligation he never wanted.

Before the school prize-giving, Gussie consumes far more alcohol than intended. Instead of remaining a silent observer while Bertie speaks, he takes the platform himself and delivers an uninhibited address that mocks the dignitaries, criticizes the prize winners, and exposes private feelings. The occasion becomes a public disaster. Madeline is appalled by his behavior and withdraws from him, activating Bertie's fear that she will regard him as her alternative. The romantic problems that Bertie meant to solve are now worse, and the disorder also spreads through Brinkley Court as hungry and agitated guests act on his increasingly desperate advice.

Late-night maneuvers and misunderstandings around the household offend Anatole, who threatens to leave Brinkley Court. Aunt Dahlia faces the loss of the chef on whom much of her domestic happiness depends, Gussie and Madeline are estranged, Angela and Tuppy remain at odds, and Bertie is in danger of being taken seriously as Madeline's reserve husband. Bertie finally abandons his claim to manage the crisis alone and lets Jeeves direct the conclusion. Jeeves brings Gussie and Madeline back together, helps Angela and Tuppy reconcile, and removes the threat of Anatole's departure. With Madeline safely engaged to Gussie, Bertie is free. He admits Jeeves's superior judgment and gives way over the white mess jacket; the offending garment is subsequently destroyed, leaving their familiar partnership restored.

characters.description: A young mongoose swept from his burrow by a flood and taken in by an English family in India. Curious, bold, and instinctively hostile to snakes, he explores the bungalow and garden before defending the household from the cobras that claim the grounds.
characters.name: Rikki-Tikki-Tavi

characters.description: The young son of the family that rescues Rikki after the flood. He quickly treats the mongoose as a pet and companion, and his safety becomes one of Rikki's chief concerns when the snakes threaten the bungalow.
characters.name: Teddy

characters.description: Teddy's father, an Englishman living with his family in a bungalow in India. He recognizes that a mongoose can protect a house from snakes and uses his gun when Rikki attacks Nag in the bathroom.
characters.name: Teddy's Father

characters.description: Teddy's mother, who is initially anxious about allowing a wild mongoose near her son. Rikki's defense of Teddy and the household earns her gratitude and trust.
characters.name: Alice

characters.description: A large male cobra who lives in the garden with Nagaina and regards the human family as an obstacle to their control of the grounds. He attempts to surprise Rikki during their first meeting and later enters the bungalow to wait for Teddy's father.
characters.name: Nag

characters.description: Nag's mate, a dangerous female cobra whose eggs are hidden in the garden. She plots with Nag against the household and, after his death, directly threatens Teddy while trying to preserve her last egg.
characters.name: Nagaina

characters.description: A tailorbird who lives in the garden with his mate. He mourns a fledgling killed by Nag and supplies Rikki with information about the cobras, although fear sometimes makes him reluctant to act.
characters.name: Darzee

characters.description: Darzee's practical and courageous mate. Understanding the danger posed by Nagaina's eggs, she helps Rikki by drawing the female cobra away from the nest and later distracts her again near the veranda.
characters.name: Darzee's Wife

characters.description: A timid muskrat who creeps around the bungalow at night. His anxious hints alert Rikki that Nag and Nagaina are moving near the house, helping the mongoose locate the greater danger.
characters.name: Chuchundra

recaps.ending: After killing Nag, Rikki learns that Nagaina's eggs are close to hatching. With help from Darzee's wife, he reaches the nest and destroys all but one egg. Nagaina is threatening Teddy at the family's breakfast table when Rikki arrives carrying the last egg. He uses it to draw her away from the boy, but she seizes it and escapes into her burrow. Rikki follows despite the danger of fighting a cobra underground. He eventually emerges and announces that Nagaina is dead and the egg will never hatch. The garden's animals celebrate the end of the cobra threat, while Rikki remains with Teddy's family and continues guarding the bungalow against snakes.
recaps.in_short: A flood carries the young mongoose Rikki-Tikki-Tavi into the garden of an English family in India. Teddy and his parents revive him and welcome him into their bungalow. Rikki soon meets Nag and Nagaina, a pair of cobras who want the family gone, and proves himself by killing a smaller snake that approaches Teddy. Warned that Nag has entered the house, Rikki attacks him in the bathroom, where Teddy's father shoots the cobra. Nagaina remains dangerous, and her hidden eggs are nearly ready to hatch. Rikki destroys most of them, then confronts her while she holds Teddy at her mercy. Using the last egg as a lure, he chases Nagaina into her burrow and kills her underground. With both cobras and their brood gone, the family and garden are safe, and Rikki settles into his role as their vigilant protector.

recaps.text: A flood washes a young mongoose named Rikki-Tikki-Tavi from his home into the garden of an English family in India. Teddy and his parents revive him, and the curious mongoose begins exploring their bungalow and grounds. In the garden he meets the tailorbird Darzee and learns that the cobras Nag and Nagaina have killed one of Darzee's young. The snakes want the human family removed so they can dominate the garden. Rikki kills a smaller venomous snake that threatens Teddy, then learns that Nag has entered the bathroom to wait for Teddy's father. Rikki attacks Nag, and the father shoots the cobra. He next discovers that Nagaina has a clutch of eggs nearly ready to hatch. Helped by Darzee's wife, Rikki destroys all but one. When Nagaina corners Teddy at breakfast, Rikki displays the surviving egg and draws her away. She takes it and flees underground, with Rikki in pursuit. He returns alive after killing her in the burrow and ensuring the last egg cannot hatch. The household and garden celebrate, and Rikki remains with the family as their protector.

characters.description: The youngest of the Ingleside children, not quite fifteen when the book opens, pretty, vain of her looks, and the only Blythe with no ambition beyond a few years of parties and good times before she settles down. She is sensitive about the slight lisp that comes back when she is agitated, hates responsibility, and has never been asked to be useful in her life. Her elder brothers and sisters are grown and mostly away at college; she is still a schoolgirl at home with her mother and Susan.
characters.name: Rilla Blythe

characters.description: Mistress of Ingleside, with a grown family scattered between home and college. She is happy, settled, and, at the opening of the book, chiefly occupied with her children's futures and the ordinary business of the Glen.
characters.name: Anne Blythe

characters.description: The doctor at Glen St. Mary, long established in his practice, and the steady centre of the Ingleside household.
characters.name: Gilbert Blythe

characters.description: The Ingleside housekeeper of many years, elderly now, fiercely devoted to the family, and the household's most reliable source of opinion. She reads the newspaper aloud, argues with the world, and refuses on principle to be discouraged by anything.
characters.name: Susan Baker

characters.description: Once Miss Cornelia Bryant of Four Winds, now Mrs. Marshall Elliott of the Glen, still blunt and still practical, and a constant visitor at the Ingleside kitchen with the news of the district.
characters.name: Mrs. Marshall Elliott

characters.description: The eldest Blythe son, just finished at Redmond and about to begin medicine, red-haired, energetic, and impatient for something worth doing. He is quietly attached to Faith Meredith and owns a small brown-and-white dog who will not leave his side.
characters.name: Jem Blythe

characters.description: The second Blythe son, home from Redmond after an illness, beautiful, dreamy, and a poet. He loves the valley, hates ugliness and cruelty more than most people can understand, and has always been closer to Rilla than any of the others. Years ago he told the children that he had seen the Pied Piper coming over the hills.
characters.name: Walter Blythe

characters.description: The quiet Blythe son, brown and self-contained, still a schoolboy at the opening of the book and Susan's particular charge since his difficult infancy. He says little and thinks a good deal.
characters.name: Shirley Blythe

characters.description: A schoolteacher who boards at Ingleside, some fifteen years older than Rilla and her closest confidante. Dark, clever, and given to moods, she is engaged to a man working abroad and is troubled by vivid dreams she believes to be prophetic.
characters.name: Gertrude Oliver

characters.description: The son of Owen and Leslie Ford of the little house on Four Winds Harbour, a visitor to the Glen in the summers, older than Rilla and much admired by every girl in the district. Easy, teasing, and well travelled, he takes notice of Rilla at her first grown-up party.
characters.name: Kenneth Ford

characters.description: The eldest of the manse children, now grown, a beautiful and warm-hearted young woman studying at Redmond, still as fearless and impulsive as she was as a child, and long understood to belong to Jem Blythe.
characters.name: Faith Meredith

characters.description: The quieter Meredith daughter, gentle, watchful, and reserved, who keeps house at the manse and keeps her own feelings entirely to herself.
characters.name: Una Meredith

characters.description: Brought up by Mrs. Marshall Elliott since she was found as a runaway child, and now a young woman of the Glen, still plain-spoken to the point of rudeness, engaged to a local man and full of the district's news.
characters.name: Mary Vance

characters.description: Jem Blythe's small, ugly, devoted dog, who follows him everywhere and is uneasy whenever his master is out of sight.
characters.name: Dog Monday

characters.description: A newborn baby whose mother has died and whose father has gone overseas, found by Rilla in a wretched house up the Glen and carried home in a soup tureen because there was nothing else to put him in. He is sickly, ugly, and entirely unwanted by anyone else.
characters.name: James Kitchener Anderson

characters.description: A prosperous, disagreeable Glen farmer with long whiskers, known throughout the district by an unflattering nickname, who holds and loudly airs opinions that set him against most of his neighbours.
characters.name: Mr. Pryor

characters.description: Mr. Pryor's daughter, a pale, timid, colourless girl of Rilla's acquaintance who has never in her life stood up to her father, and who is in love with a young man of the Glen.
characters.name: Miranda Pryor

characters.description: The small son of the minister and his second wife, a solemn, intense child who takes everything he is told with complete literalness and feels things far beyond his years.
characters.name: Bruce Meredith

recaps.ending: The war ends. Jem Blythe, missing for months, is found to have been a prisoner in Germany, escapes, and comes home lame but alive, and Dog Monday's long vigil at the station platform ends when he finally meets the right train. Jerry Meredith recovers from his wound and Carl Meredith comes home having lost an eye. Shirley returns from the flying corps. Susan Baker, having refused a proposal of marriage during the war, takes a modest holiday of her own at the end of it. Gertrude Oliver is married to her fiancé. Jims's father comes back from France, marries again, and takes the boy, so Rilla gives up the child she raised from a soup tureen and finds she has grown up in the process. Walter is not among the returning. His mother, his family, and Una Meredith, who never told anyone what she felt for him, carry that loss into the peace, and his last poem has made him known far beyond the Glen. Kenneth Ford comes back at last and walks up to Ingleside, and when he asks Rilla whether she has kept the promise she made him the night before he sailed, her old childhood lisp returns in her answer. Rilla ends the book engaged, and the Glen begins the long work of living afterwards.
recaps.in_short: Rilla Blythe is not quite fifteen and wants nothing but a few years of parties when the First World War begins on the night of her first grown-up dance. Over the next four years the war takes her brothers and her friends: Jem enlists at once, Jerry Meredith with him, and Walter, held back at first by illness and then tormented for not going, enlists in his turn. Rilla, who has never been useful in her life, brings home an orphaned newborn in a soup tureen and raises him, founds and runs a Junior Red Cross, and learns to wait and work while the casualty lists come in. Jem's dog takes up a station-platform vigil that lasts the whole war. Walter is killed at the front, and his last letter to Rilla asks her not to grieve. Later Jem is reported wounded and missing, and the family lives for months in uncertainty before learning that he is a prisoner and has escaped. The armistice comes; Jem, Shirley, Jerry, and Carl come home, Walter does not, and Rilla, grown up, is claimed by Kenneth Ford.

recaps.text: Previously: Anne Shirley, brought up as an orphan at Green Gables in Avonlea, married Doctor Gilbert Blythe and has raised their family at Ingleside in Glen St. Mary, with the housekeeper Susan Baker and the old friend once known as Miss Cornelia Bryant, now Mrs. Marshall Elliott, close at hand. The Blythe children are Jem, Walter, the twins Nan and Di, Shirley, and the youngest, Rilla. Their closest friends are the children of the Glen manse: Jerry, Faith, Una, and Carl Meredith, whose widowed father, the Reverend John Meredith, married Rosemary West after a long delay caused by a promise Rosemary had made to her sister. As children the two families spent their summers in a wooded hollow they called Rainbow Valley, where Walter once told them he had seen the Pied Piper coming over the hills and they promised to follow when he called. The elder children are now grown and mostly away at Redmond College. This book opens in the summer of 1914.

Rilla Blythe, the youngest at Ingleside and not yet fifteen, is looking forward to four carefree years before she need think about anything. The household gathers for the summer: Jem home from Redmond and quietly attached to Faith Meredith, Walter recovering from typhoid, Nan and Di, Shirley, and Gertrude Oliver, the schoolteacher who boards at Ingleside and is Rilla's confidante. Gertrude is uneasy over a dream she cannot explain. Rilla goes to her first grown-up party, a dance at the Four Winds lighthouse, wearing her first long dress, and is noticed by Kenneth Ford. In the middle of the evening word arrives that Britain has declared war on Germany, and the young men talk of nothing else. Rilla, whose slippers have been taken as a joke, walks home barefoot and humiliated, and afterwards remembers that night as the last of the old world.

Jem enlists in the first days, along with Jerry Meredith, and the Glen begins to divide between those who are going and those who are not. Walter, still weak from illness, cannot go, and takes his exclusion harder than anyone guesses. When Jem's train pulls out, his dog follows it to the station and refuses to come home, settling in the shed by the platform to watch every train that comes in, and there he stays. Sent up the Glen on an errand, Rilla finds a newborn baby in a wretched house where the mother has died and the father has gone overseas, and carries the child home in a soup tureen for want of anything else. Challenged by her mother to take the responsibility or give it up, she keeps him, names him Jims, and begins to learn from a book how to raise a baby. She also founds a Junior Red Cross among the Glen girls and finds herself its president.

The war settles into a long ordeal at home. Susan reads the despatches aloud and follows the fighting on a map; every reverse is argued over in the Ingleside kitchen and every list of casualties is read with dread. Jem writes from the front. Rilla struggles with Jims, who thrives despite her inexperience, and with the Junior Red Cross, which teaches her to organize, to endure disagreeable people, and to finish what she begins. The heavy Canadian losses in the spring fighting bring the war home to the Glen for the first time, and the district begins to count its own dead. Walter, well again, is bitterly conscious that he has not enlisted; he is talked about, and one day he receives an envelope containing a white feather. He says nothing about it to his family, and Rilla, who understands him better than anyone, watches him with growing fear.

Walter decides to enlist and tells Rilla first, out in the valley. He explains that he is going precisely because he is afraid, that he could not live with staying at home, and that he has no illusions about what he is going to. Anne bears it without protest, and Rilla promises him that she will not cry when he goes and will keep her courage while he is away. Walter trains, and then sails. Una Meredith says goodbye to him and keeps to herself what it costs her. Ingleside settles into the routine of waiting: letters, parcels, Red Cross work, and the newspaper. Rilla is no longer the girl who wanted only a good time; she runs her committee, raises Jims, and holds herself together in public. Kenneth Ford, before he goes overseas himself, comes to Ingleside to say goodbye and asks Rilla for a promise she keeps privately and takes entirely seriously.

Rilla takes on the affairs of a timid Glen girl whose father, who is against the war, has forbidden her to marry her soldier before he sails; Rilla arranges the wedding herself, in the man's own house, and carries it off. Life at home goes on in a mixture of small comedy and constant dread. Then, one night, Jem's dog howls at the station, and the household knows without being told that something has happened. Word follows that Walter has been killed in action in France. His last letter reaches Rilla afterwards: he tells her that he had known he would not come back, that he was not afraid at the end, and that she is not to grieve for him but to keep her courage. Rilla does not cry. The poem Walter wrote at the front is published and read across the country. Ingleside goes on, and Anne, after a long illness of grief, gets up again because the others need her.

The war drags into its worst years. Shirley turns eighteen and enlists in the flying corps, and his mother has to let another son go. Carl Meredith is at the front and Jerry Meredith is badly wounded. Susan Baker receives, and briskly refuses, a proposal of marriage from a neighbour she despises. The great German advance in the spring brings the Glen its blackest Sunday, when the news seems to leave no hope at all and only Susan refuses to admit defeat. Then Ingleside is told that Jem has been wounded and is missing, and there the matter rests: month after month passes with no word whether he is alive or dead, while his dog keeps his place at the station. Rilla, hardened and entirely grown up, keeps the household and her mother going. Faith Meredith, nursing overseas, waits as they all wait.

Word comes at last that Jem is alive, a prisoner in Germany. He escapes, and in time he comes home, lame and much altered but himself, and his dog's long watch on the station platform is over. The tide turns on the western front, and the armistice is celebrated in the Glen with bells and bonfires. Carl Meredith returns having lost an eye, Jerry recovers, and Shirley comes back from the flying corps. Susan takes a modest holiday of her own, and Gertrude Oliver is married. Jims's father comes home from France, marries again, and claims his son, so Rilla gives up the child she raised and understands how much the four years have made of her. Walter does not return, and his family and Una Meredith carry that with them into the peace. Kenneth Ford comes back at last and walks up to Ingleside, and when he asks Rilla whether she kept the promise she made him before he sailed, the lisp of her childhood comes back in her answer. The book ends with Rilla engaged and the Glen beginning again.

characters.description: The young prince of the peaceful island kingdom of Pingaree. Inga has been sheltered from danger, but an invasion forces him to act with courage, patience, and growing judgment as he tries to rescue his parents and their people.
characters.name: Prince Inga

characters.description: Inga's father and the kindly ruler of Pingaree. He has guarded three magic pearls entrusted to his family and explains their powers to Inga when danger threatens the island.
characters.name: King Kitticut

characters.description: The queen of Pingaree and Inga's mother. She shares the island's quiet royal life until the northern invasion breaks up the family and places the kingdom in captivity.
characters.name: Queen Garee

characters.description: The round, cheerful king of Gilgad, visiting Pingaree with a hearty appetite and a store of songs and stories. Rinkitink dislikes solemnity, but beneath his playful talk he is affectionate and loyal to Inga.
characters.name: King Rinkitink

characters.description: Rinkitink's surly talking goat and usual mount. Bilbil complains about nearly everything, answers the king's cheerfulness with sharp remarks, and nevertheless remains part of the little company.
characters.name: Bilbil

characters.description: The harsh ruler of Regos, one of the twin islands north of Pingaree. Gos leads the invasion, seizes Pingaree's wealth, and carries its people away to labor as captives.
characters.name: King Gos

characters.description: The clever and cruel queen of Coregos, sister island to Regos. Cor relies on trickery when force fails and watches closely for the source of Inga's unexpected success.
characters.name: Queen Cor

characters.description: The kind daughter of a poor charcoal burner. Zella carries supplies to Queen Cor and, despite her humble place, becomes an important friend to Inga when he most needs help.
characters.name: Zella

characters.description: Zella's honest, independent father, who earns his living burning charcoal. Nikobob wants no reward that would make him responsible for ruling others and values his simple home over a crown.
characters.name: Nikobob

characters.description: The current ruler of the underground Nome Kingdom. Kaliko receives the fleeing rulers of Regos and Coregos, then uses his own power and bargains to obstruct Inga's rescue.
characters.name: Kaliko

characters.description: A girl from the Emerald City and one of Ozma's closest companions. Dorothy comes to the Nome Kingdom when Ozma learns of Inga's trouble, bringing friendly determination and the authority of Oz behind the rescue.
characters.name: Dorothy Gale

characters.description: Ozma's inventive court magician. The Wizard accompanies Dorothy, studies the enchantments surrounding the captives, and brings skill as well as magic to the final rescue.
characters.name: The Wizard of Oz

characters.description: A prince of Boboland who has spent years hidden by an enchantment. The Wizard recognizes that the ill-tempered goat Bilbil is not what he appears and restores the prince's proper form.
characters.name: Prince Bobo

recaps.ending: Dorothy and the Wizard reach the Nome Kingdom under Ozma's authority and end Kaliko's attempt to keep the royal captives. King Kitticut and Queen Garee are freed, and the Wizard also breaks the old enchantment on Bilbil, restoring him as Prince Bobo of Boboland. Inga, Rinkitink, Bobo, and the rescued rulers visit the Emerald City as Ozma's guests before returning to Pingaree. The people of Pingaree are brought home, the island is rebuilt, and the magic pearls remain with its royal house. Rinkitink would happily prolong his visit, but representatives from Gilgad finally arrive to carry their king back to his neglected duties. Inga's courage has proved him ready for the responsibilities that will one day be his.
recaps.in_short: When warriors from Regos and Coregos conquer Pingaree and enslave its people, young Prince Inga escapes with visiting King Rinkitink and Rinkitink's talking goat, Bilbil. Guided and protected by three magic pearls, Inga crosses the sea, defeats the invaders, and frees many captives. Queen Cor steals the pearls for a time, but the charcoal burner's daughter Zella helps Inga recover them. The enemy rulers flee with Inga's parents to the underground Nome Kingdom, where Kaliko tries to prevent their release. Dorothy and the Wizard arrive from Oz, free the captives, and uncover Bilbil's true identity as the enchanted Prince Bobo. Pingaree is restored, while the reluctant Rinkitink is eventually fetched home to rule Gilgad.

recaps.text: Ozma rules the peaceful fairyland of Oz with Dorothy and the Wizard among her friends. The underground Nome Kingdom has troubled Oz before, although Kaliko now occupies its throne. This adventure begins on Pingaree, outside Oz, with a new royal family and the visiting King Rinkitink.

Prince Inga lives on the prosperous island of Pingaree with King Kitticut and Queen Garee. Their guest, the merry King Rinkitink of Gilgad, arrives with his bad-tempered talking goat Bilbil. Kitticut tells Inga the secret of three pearls: one grants strength, one protects its bearer, and one offers wise counsel. Soon warriors from Regos and Coregos invade. Pingaree is plundered, its people and rulers are carried away, and Inga, Rinkitink, and Bilbil are left behind. With the pearls hidden in his shoes, Inga gains the power and guidance needed to act. A magic boat carries the three survivors north as the young prince sets out to recover his parents and free his kingdom.

The magic boat brings Inga's party to the twin islands of Regos and Coregos. Protected and strengthened by the pearls, Inga defeats forces that greatly outnumber him and releases Pingaree's enslaved people. Queen Cor cannot overcome him openly, so she watches for the secret of his power. Rinkitink innocently moves the prince's shoes, allowing Cor to steal them and leaving Inga without the pearls when he believes he needs them most. Zella, the kind daughter of the charcoal burner Nikobob, is sent on errands to the queen and befriends the prince. With her help, and with Bilbil's noisy interference, Inga recovers the shoes and their hidden magic. The friends escape Cor's control, but the rulers responsible for the invasion still hold Inga's parents.

Once Inga regains the pearls, the power of Regos and Coregos collapses. Nikobob refuses an offered crown, preferring his independent life, and the freed people prepare to rebuild. King Gos and Queen Cor flee with King Kitticut and Queen Garee to the underground Nome Kingdom. Inga, Rinkitink, and Bilbil follow them and confront Kaliko, the Nome King. Kaliko shelters the fugitives and tries to bargain for Inga's magic, then uses enchantment and deception to keep the captives out of reach. Even the white pearl's counsel and the companions' courage cannot easily overcome the Nome King's underground power, leaving Inga at the end of another contest that strength alone cannot settle.

Dorothy and the Wizard arrive in the Nome Kingdom with Ozma's backing. Kaliko yields, and King Kitticut and Queen Garee are freed. The Wizard also discovers that Bilbil is really Prince Bobo of Boboland under an old enchantment and restores his human form. Ozma welcomes the whole company to a banquet in the Emerald City before Inga returns with his parents and people to Pingaree. The island kingdom is restored, the three pearls remain in the royal family's keeping, and Inga has shown that he can meet danger with courage and judgment. Rinkitink tries to remain with his friends rather than resume the tiresome business of governing, but a delegation from Gilgad finally arrives and carries its wandering king home.

characters.description: A good-natured villager in the Catskill Mountains who readily helps his neighbors but avoids the work needed to maintain his own farm. Harried by domestic conflict, he prefers wandering with his dog, fishing, and talking with the village regulars. One mountain excursion carries him away from everything familiar.
characters.name: Rip Van Winkle

characters.description: Rip's forceful wife, who repeatedly confronts him about his idleness, the declining farm, and the state of their household. Rip escapes their arguments by leaving home for the village or the mountains.
characters.name: Dame Van Winkle

characters.description: Rip's daughter. She is a child when he goes into the mountains and a grown mother by the time he returns, making her one of the clearest signs of how much of his life has passed without him.
characters.name: Judith Gardenier

characters.description: Rip's son, who grows into a young man closely resembling his father and sharing his reluctance to work. Rip sees him before understanding who he is.
characters.name: Rip Van Winkle Jr.

characters.description: The elderly innkeeper and presiding figure among the village regulars before Rip's disappearance. He spends long days beneath the inn's tree, quietly signaling his opinions while the others discuss old newspapers and local affairs.
characters.name: Nicholas Vedder

characters.description: The village schoolmaster, who reads news aloud and supplies learned commentary to the group at the inn. The changed village later remembers him as a soldier and public official of the Revolutionary era.
characters.name: Derrick Van Bummel

characters.description: An old resident descended from a historian of the region. When Rip's strange account causes confusion, Peter identifies an established local tradition about Hendrick Hudson and his crew returning periodically to the Catskills.
characters.name: Peter Vanderdonk

characters.description: A solemn man in old-fashioned Dutch clothing whom Rip meets high in the mountains. He carries a keg and silently leads Rip to a secluded gathering whose uncanny drink brings on an extraordinarily long sleep.
characters.name: The Mountain Stranger

recaps.ending: Rip returns to his village after sleeping through twenty years and at first cannot make sense of its unfamiliar people, buildings, and political arguments. He learns that the American colonies have become an independent nation, that his wife has died, and that many of his former companions are dead or scattered. His grown daughter Judith recognizes him and takes him into her home, while his son has become an idle young man much like him. Peter Vanderdonk's account of Hendrick Hudson's crew gives the community a traditional explanation for Rip's mountain encounter, and Rip's age and familiar face eventually establish his identity. With his family obligations changed and his long absence accepted, he resumes his old habit of sitting among the villagers, now telling his extraordinary story to visitors and becoming a local authority on life before the Revolution.
recaps.in_short: Easygoing Rip Van Winkle neglects his farm, helps his neighbors, and retreats from arguments with his wife into the Catskill Mountains. There he follows a strangely dressed man to a silent group playing at bowls, drinks their liquor, and falls asleep. He wakes to find his gun decayed, his beard long, and his dog gone. Back in the village, everything has changed: twenty years have passed, the Revolution has replaced British rule with the United States, and the political language around him is unfamiliar. Rip discovers that his wife and several old companions are dead, while his children are grown. His daughter Judith takes him in, and an old local tradition links the mountain figures to Hendrick Hudson's crew. Accepted as the same Rip who vanished, he settles into old age as a village storyteller, spared the domestic and economic responsibilities he once avoided.

recaps.text: Rip Van Winkle lives in a Dutch settlement near the Catskills before the American Revolution. He is generous with neighbors and children but neglects his own farm, and his wife's repeated complaints drive him toward the inn or the woods. During a mountain walk with his dog, Rip meets a man in old Dutch clothing carrying a keg. He helps the stranger reach a secluded hollow, where silent figures play at bowls. Rip drinks their liquor and falls asleep. On waking, he finds his beard grown, his gun rusted, and his dog missing. The village below is larger and unfamiliar, its old inn replaced and its residents arguing about elections and citizenship rather than King George. Rip gradually learns that twenty years have passed and the colonies have become the United States. His wife and several companions are dead, his children are adults, and his daughter Judith gives him a home. Peter Vanderdonk connects Rip's account to local stories that Hendrick Hudson's crew returns to the mountains. Once the villagers accept Rip's identity, he becomes a familiar elderly storyteller whose memories preserve the community that existed before the Revolution.

characters.description: A good-natured Catskill villager who helps his neighbors but neglects his own farm. Seeking relief from domestic arguments, he wanders into the mountains and encounters a strange company whose drink separates him from the world he knows.
characters.name: Rip Van Winkle

characters.description: Rip's forceful wife, who repeatedly confronts him about his idleness, the failing farm, and the neglected household. Rip habitually escapes their disputes by going to the village or the mountains.
characters.name: Dame Van Winkle

characters.description: Rip's daughter, a child when he disappears into the mountains and a grown mother when he returns. She recognizes him and provides him with a family home in the transformed village.
characters.name: Judith Gardenier

characters.description: The elderly innkeeper and presiding figure among the village regulars before Rip's disappearance. He sits beneath the inn's tree while the group discusses old news and local concerns.
characters.name: Nicholas Vedder

characters.description: The village schoolmaster, who reads news to the inn's regulars and provides learned commentary. The changed village later remembers his service during the Revolution and his public career.
characters.name: Derrick Van Bummel

characters.description: An elderly resident whose family preserves local history. He explains the Catskill tradition that Hendrick Hudson and his crew periodically return to the mountains, giving the village a way to understand Rip's account.
characters.name: Peter Vanderdonk

characters.description: A solemn stranger in old-fashioned Dutch clothes whom Rip meets in the mountains. He carries a keg and leads Rip to a silent gathering where an uncanny drink induces a sleep lasting many years.
characters.name: The Mountain Stranger

characters.description: A lanky Connecticut schoolmaster who teaches and boards among the Dutch farming families of Sleepy Hollow. Educated but highly superstitious, he is fascinated by ghost stories and hopes to improve his circumstances by marrying Katrina Van Tassel.
characters.name: Ichabod Crane

characters.description: The only child of the prosperous Baltus Van Tassel. Sociable and expected to inherit a rich farm, she draws several suitors. Ichabod's courtship is tied closely to the comfortable future he imagines on her family's property.
characters.name: Katrina Van Tassel

characters.description: A strong, confident horseman known for practical jokes and physical skill. As Katrina's leading local suitor, he responds to Ichabod's courtship with rivalry, intimidation, and mischief.
characters.name: Brom Bones

characters.description: Katrina's wealthy father and the hospitable owner of a flourishing farm. His barns, livestock, fields, and well-stocked table represent the prosperity that Ichabod hopes to enter through marriage.
characters.name: Baltus Van Tassel

characters.description: A farmer lodging Ichabod at the time of the Van Tassels' gathering. He lends the schoolmaster his gaunt, difficult horse for the evening journey.
characters.name: Hans Van Ripper

characters.description: Hans Van Ripper's stubborn old horse, loaned to Ichabod for his visit to the Van Tassel farm. His awkward pace and uncertain responses complicate the schoolmaster's fearful ride home.
characters.name: Gunpowder

characters.description: The spectral rider said to be a Hessian soldier decapitated by a cannonball during the Revolution. Sleepy Hollow tradition holds that he rides at night seeking his head and disappears near the church bridge and burial ground.
characters.name: The Headless Horseman

recaps.ending: The collection closes with Ichabod Crane's disappearance after his night ride from the Van Tassel farm. Pursued by what appears to be the Headless Horseman, he is struck by the rider's thrown head near the church bridge. The next day searchers find the borrowed horse, Ichabod's hat, and a broken pumpkin, but not Ichabod. Brom Bones soon marries Katrina and reacts knowingly when the pumpkin is discussed, strongly implying that he staged the apparition to drive away his rival. Later news says Ichabod survived, made a life elsewhere, studied law, entered politics, and became a judge. Sleepy Hollow's traditional storytellers nevertheless retain the supernatural version, adding the abandoned schoolhouse to their haunted landscape. This ending complements Rip Van Winkle's earlier return: Rip is absorbed into his changed home as a keeper of old memories, while Ichabod leaves his community and becomes the subject of the legend that remains behind.
recaps.in_short: Two tales place personal upheaval within legendary communities along the Hudson. In the first, idle but kindly Rip Van Winkle follows a strange man into the Catskills, drinks with a silent company, and sleeps for twenty years. He returns after the American Revolution to find his wife dead, his children grown, and his village transformed. His daughter takes him in, and he becomes a teller of the old world he remembers. In the second, superstitious schoolmaster Ichabod Crane courts the wealthy Katrina Van Tassel in rivalry with prankster Brom Bones. After a gathering filled with ghost stories, a headless rider chases Ichabod and strikes him with a thrown object. Ichabod vanishes, leaving a broken pumpkin as evidence. Brom marries Katrina and appears to know more than he admits; reports later place Ichabod alive and successful elsewhere, though Sleepy Hollow preserves the haunting as legend.

recaps.text: In the collection's first tale, Rip Van Winkle is a generous but idle villager living near the Catskills before the American Revolution. Avoiding his neglected farm and disputes with his wife, he wanders into the mountains, where a strangely dressed man leads him to a silent group playing at bowls. Rip drinks their liquor and falls asleep. He wakes with a long beard and a rusted gun, then returns to a village he barely recognizes. Twenty years have passed. The colonies have become the United States, political debate has replaced loyalty to King George, and Rip's old companions are dead or scattered. His wife has died and his children have grown; his daughter Judith recognizes him and offers him a home. An old local tradition associates Rip's mysterious companions with Hendrick Hudson's crew. Accepted by the community, Rip settles into old age as a storyteller whose memories connect the new village with the world before the Revolution.

Rip Van Winkle has returned from a twenty-year supernatural sleep to a post-Revolutionary village, where his grown daughter takes him in and he becomes a teller of the former community. The second tale moves to Sleepy Hollow, where lanky schoolmaster Ichabod Crane boards with local farming families and eagerly listens to ghost stories. He courts Katrina Van Tassel, whose wealthy father's farm appeals to his ambitions, while the strong prankster Brom Bones competes for her. At a gathering at the Van Tassel home, the guests tell stories of the Headless Horseman. Ichabod later leaves dejected after speaking privately with Katrina. Riding through the dark on a borrowed horse, he is pursued by a figure that appears to carry its head. Near the church bridge, the pursuer throws the head and knocks Ichabod down. By morning Ichabod is gone; his hat and a broken pumpkin remain. Brom soon marries Katrina and seems amused by the pumpkin detail, implying that he played the ghost. Reports eventually place Ichabod alive and professionally successful elsewhere, but the neighborhood continues to tell his disappearance as a supernatural legend.

characters.description: A survivor of Calis's Novindus expedition who returns to Krondor determined to become rich before the coming war overturns the Kingdom. Roo begins with little capital but an exact memory for prices, a talent for reading desire, and a willingness to treat reputation, credit, and information as goods that can be traded.
characters.name: Rupert Avery

characters.description: Roo's closest friend, once a Ravensburg blacksmith's apprentice and now a proven soldier in Calis's service. Erik understands the scale of the invasion being prepared in Novindus and chooses continued military duty, placing him on a different path from Roo without ending their loyalty to one another.
characters.name: Erik von Darkmoor

characters.description: A veteran swordsman who survived the expedition with Erik and Roo. Luis moves comfortably between military and civilian society and becomes one of the friends Roo can trust while building a life in Krondor.
characters.name: Luis de Savona

characters.description: An ageing former thief who rose to become Duke of Krondor and one of the Kingdom's most experienced administrators. James knows that Calis's warning is genuine and begins preparing a city whose merchants and nobles would rather treat the danger as distant.
characters.name: Duke James

characters.description: The commander of the Novindus mission and the son of Tomas and Queen Aglaranna. Calis carries human, elven, and Valheru inheritances and has spent years tracing the force behind the Emerald Queen. He returns to the field while the Kingdom makes practical use of his warning.
characters.name: Calis

characters.description: An Isalani gambler and wanderer who denies the existence of magic while performing feats nobody around him can explain. Beneath the jokes and apparent disorder, Nakor has a serious interest in the unnatural powers surrounding the Emerald Queen's campaign.
characters.name: Nakor

characters.description: A practical young woman whose steadiness contrasts with Roo's restless ambition. Karli offers him affection, a household, and a connection to the respectable commercial world he wants to enter, while seeing more clearly than he does what his hunger for status may cost.
characters.name: Karli

characters.description: One of Krondor's established merchant powers, wealthy enough to shape markets and backed by the reputation and connections Roo is trying to acquire. Esterbrook takes an interest in the ambitious newcomer when their commercial paths begin to cross.
characters.name: Jacob Esterbrook

characters.description: Jacob Esterbrook's beautiful and socially assured daughter. Sylvia moves through Krondor's wealthy circles with an ease Roo covets and becomes inseparable in his mind from the success and acceptance he is trying to purchase.
characters.name: Sylvia Esterbrook

characters.description: The former orphan of Crydee who became a Great One of Kelewan. Pug is now an elder magician investigating the forces behind the invasion, following evidence that reaches beyond Midkemia and ordinary spellcraft.
characters.name: Pug

characters.description: A formidable magician who appears to know both Pug and the threat he is pursuing. Miranda is independent, secretive, and able to cross dangers that would defeat most practitioners, but she gives Pug help before she gives him a complete explanation of her motives.
characters.name: Miranda

characters.description: The general directing the Emerald Queen's conquered peoples and armies. Fadawah is methodical rather than fanatical, turning victory in Novindus into the ships, supplies, and command structure needed for a campaign across the sea.
characters.name: Fadawah

recaps.ending: Roo emerges from the commercial struggle as one of Krondor's merchant princes. He has survived efforts by established rivals to use his appetite for Sylvia and his dependence on credit against him, and he converts foreknowledge of war, control of scarce goods, and a willingness to risk everything into a fortune. The achievement carries a personal cost: Karli has seen his infidelity and self-deception, while Roo has learned that wealth does not make him accepted by the old commercial families or free him from their methods. Erik remains in Calis's military service, helping prepare for the attack both friends know is coming. In Novindus, Fadawah has completed the practical work of turning conquest into invasion; the Emerald Queen's forces are ready to sail. Pug's investigation confirms that demons are not merely battlefield creatures but part of the power moving behind the campaign. Miranda intervenes to bring him back from that danger, becoming an uneasy ally while leaving her deeper history unrevealed. The Kingdom ends the book richer in warning and resources but almost out of time.
recaps.in_short: After surviving Novindus, Rupert Avery returns to Krondor and sets out to build a fortune while Erik stays with Calis's soldiers. Roo starts at the edge of the city's trading world, uses information and credit boldly, marries the practical Karli, and expands through increasingly dangerous bargains. His success brings him into the orbit of the powerful merchant Jacob Esterbrook and Esterbrook's daughter Sylvia. Roo's attraction to Sylvia becomes both a betrayal of Karli and a weakness his rivals can exploit. He suffers financial reverses but uses his knowledge that invasion is approaching to anticipate shortages, gamble on essential goods, and rebuild on a larger scale, ending as a merchant prince able to support the Kingdom's preparations. Meanwhile Calis, Nakor, Pug, and Miranda pursue the supernatural side of the threat. Fadawah finishes assembling the Emerald Queen's invasion fleet, and Pug learns that demonic powers stand behind more than isolated monsters. The coming war joins Roo's commercial rise to the Kingdom's survival.

recaps.text: Previously, in Shadow of a Dark Queen: Erik von Darkmoor killed his abusive half-brother while defending Rosalyn and fled Ravensburg with Rupert Avery. Captured and condemned, the two were secretly recruited into Calis's company and trained by Robert de Loungville for a reconnaissance mission in Novindus. Calis, the son of Tomas and the elven queen Aglaranna, carries human, elven, and Valheru inheritances into the generation after the Riftwar. His company found a continent being consumed by the Emerald Queen's forces: a disciplined host under Fadawah that included displaced humans, Pantathian serpent priests, Saaur warriors, and summoned demons. The expedition lost many of its members but escaped with proof that Novindus was being conquered to prepare an invasion of the Kingdom. Erik and Roo returned as veterans. Pug and Tomas, now elder guardians of a world they once saved at Sethanon, know that the new threat reaches beyond ordinary war, but the Emerald Queen's true nature and ultimate objective remain uncertain.

Roo and Erik return from Novindus with pay, scars, and no possibility of resuming their old lives. Erik remains attached to Calis's military work because he understands how little time the Kingdom has to prepare. Roo chooses commerce. Krondor's established traders have capital, guild connections, and family reputations he lacks, so he begins with small bargains and information gathered in taverns, warehouses, and counting rooms. Duke James quietly treats Calis's report as a strategic warning even while most of the city continues in peacetime habits. Roo's first ventures show both his talent and his central danger: he is willing to stake tomorrow's security on a chance to advance today.

Roo moves from opportunistic dealing into organised trade, learning how merchants use credit and social confidence as aggressively as soldiers use weapons. Karli becomes part of the stable life he says he wants, while his growing reputation opens rooms previously closed to him. He encounters Jacob Esterbrook, one of the men who already commands the world Roo wants to enter, and Sylvia Esterbrook, whose beauty and assurance make her seem to embody that world. Roo reads the market well but reads his own desires badly. Each success encourages him to borrow more, expand faster, and assume that intelligence can protect him from people with longer memories and deeper reserves.

Roo's ventures spread beyond Krondor, tying him to distant suppliers, shipping schedules, and partners whose failures can become his own. He marries Karli and gains a home and a measure of respectability, yet continues to chase the approval of wealthier circles. The Esterbrooks draw closer to his business. Jacob can offer access and credit while also learning exactly where Roo is vulnerable; Sylvia encourages Roo's fascination without requiring him to confront what it means for his marriage. In parallel, Erik and Calis continue the practical preparations for invasion, reminding Roo that the market he is building in may soon be transformed by war.

Roo becomes wealthy enough to mistake rapid growth for security. His relationship with Sylvia crosses the boundary he has pretended to respect, betraying Karli and entangling business judgment with vanity. Rivals exploit his debts, obligations, and divided attention, producing a chain of reverses that threatens the structure he has built. Friends help where they can, but Roo must accept that commercial warfare is not gentler than Calis's campaigns: an opponent attacks reputation and credit because destroying either can erase a fortune without drawing a sword. The approaching invasion also begins to distort prices and supplies, turning Calis's warning into both a national emergency and the information on which Roo may make his recovery.

Roo survives the attempt to break him and uses his knowledge of the coming war to rebuild at a scale that makes him one of Krondor's leading merchants. By controlling and moving goods the Kingdom will urgently need, he turns risk into fortune and places his resources behind the defence, though neither success nor remorse immediately repairs his marriage to Karli. Erik stays with Calis's forces as the two friends' separate talents converge on the same crisis. Across the sea, Fadawah has completed the organisation of the Emerald Queen's fleet and the invasion is ready to move. Pug's investigation reaches the demon realm and confirms that the summoned creatures seen in Novindus are part of a larger supernatural design, not incidental weapons. Miranda rescues him from that danger and joins the effort without yet explaining all she knows. The Kingdom has gained money, intelligence, and preparation, but the enemy now has ships and momentum.

characters.description: An unusually advanced Tier 2 ascender training at Lenton's desert camp after helping uncover an illegal operation. Imperial attention now threatens his safety, while a Challenger deadline requires him to hunt far above his tier.
characters.name: Jiran

characters.description: Jiran's cousin and training partner at the desert camp. She has reached Molding 37 and practices with a spear while Jiran helps her apply small, controlled forces to her bones and repair the resulting injuries with mana.
characters.name: Niya

characters.description: Jiran's instructor and protector at the desert camp. He orders Jiran to avoid trouble while they await an imperial envoy, but admits that he cannot shield his pupil from the emperor. He does not condemn Jiran for killing the slavers whose actions endangered others.
characters.name: Lenton

characters.description: A noble mentor traveling with Jiran's party. He must return to Feylon instead of accompanying Jiran toward the capital, and Jiran believes his unexplained curse is responsible for the separation. Jiran is determined to search for a cure.
